questions.stem: A 64 year old man of Black African family background has had poorly controlled hypertension for 20 years. He does not have diabetes. Routine bloods show an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73m², similar to a year ago. Urine dipstick shows a trace of protein and no blood. Ultrasound shows two small, smooth kidneys of equal size.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his kidney disease?
questions.e: Long-standing poorly controlled hypertension without diabetes, with bland urine and small symmetrical kidneys, suggests hypertensive nephrosclerosis, a common cause of CKD. Renal artery stenosis gives asymmetrical kidneys.

clues: trace of protein and no blood
small, smooth kidneys of equal size
steps.x: Long-standing hypertension, bland urine, symmetrical small kidneys.

elim: Kidneys would be enlarged with multiple cysts.
He does not have diabetes.
Usually presents with haematuria in younger adults.
Usually gives asymmetrical kidney sizes.

steps.x: C: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis. Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is a common cause of CKD, second to diabetes.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has intermittent right loin pain and two episodes of visible haematuria. Her father started dialysis at 55 and her aunt had a 'brain bleed'. Her BP is 162/98 mmHg. Both kidneys are ballotable. Her eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73m² and was 55 mL/min/1.73m² four months ago.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her chronic kidney disease?
questions.e: Bilateral ballotable kidneys, haematuria, loin pain, hypertension and a family history of dialysis and intracranial haemorrhage point to ADPKD, a hereditary cause of CKD.

steps.x: Family history of kidney failure and intracranial bleeding with bilateral large kidneys.

elim: No diabetes, and kidneys would not be ballotable.
Kidneys are small, not enlarged, and there is no family pattern.
Usually unilateral, not with this family history.
Can cause pain and haematuria but not bilateral enlarged kidneys and a family history of dialysis.

steps.x: A: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. ADPKD: hereditary kidney disease, a cause of CKD; berry aneurysms cause brain bleeds.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has had several episodes of dark red urine, each starting 1 or 2 days after a sore throat. Between episodes, urine dipstick shows blood ++ and protein +. His BP is 146/90 mmHg. His eGFR has been 70 to 74 mL/min/1.73m² for a year. A renal biopsy is done.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
o: Diffuse linear IgG along the basement membrane
questions.e: Synpharyngitic haematuria (1 to 2 days after infection) with persistent haematuria and proteinuria is IgA nephropathy, a chronic glomerulonephritis that causes CKD; biopsy shows mesangial IgA. Post-streptococcal GN follows 1 to 3 weeks later.

clues: 1 or 2 days after a sore throat
steps.x: Visible haematuria 1 to 2 days after an infection with persistent haematuria and proteinuria.

elim: Anti-GBM disease, with rapidly progressive renal failure.
Diabetic nephropathy.
Would not explain persistent haematuria and proteinuria.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows 1 to 3 weeks after a sore throat.

steps.x: C: Mesangial IgA deposits. Chronic glomerulonephritis (here IgA nephropathy) is a cause of CKD; biopsy-proven chronic GN is evidence of kidney damage.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has had poor urinary stream, nocturia and a feeling of incomplete emptying for 5 years. His eGFR has fallen from 62 to 41 mL/min/1.73m² over 18 months. His bladder is palpable after voiding and is not tender. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis and a post-void residual of 900 mL.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his chronic kidney disease?
questions.e: Chronic painless retention from prostatic obstruction causes bilateral hydronephrosis and a slow decline in kidney function: obstruction is a recognised cause of CKD.

steps.x: Long-standing prostatic symptoms, painless retention, bilateral hydronephrosis.

elim: Does not cause hydronephrosis.
No diabetes, and does not cause hydronephrosis.
Does not cause hydronephrosis or a large residual.
Causes cystic enlarged kidneys, not hydronephrosis with a full bladder.

steps.x: B: Chronic bladder outflow obstruction. Obstruction is a cause of CKD; chronic painless retention causes back-pressure on both kidneys.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman had blood in her urine on a dipstick at a work health check. Repeat dipsticks over 6 months all show blood ++, and two early morning ACRs 4 months apart are 38 and 42 mg/mmol. Her eGFR has been 72 and 75 mL/min/1.73m². Cystoscopy and CT urogram are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: No kidney disease, as eGFR is above 60
questions.e: CKD is kidney damage or reduced function for 3 months or more; persistent haematuria (urological causes excluded) and albuminuria are markers of damage, so eGFR 60 to 89 with damage is stage 2.

clues: Cystoscopy and CT urogram are normal
steps.x: eGFR 60 to 89 with persistent haematuria and albuminuria for over 3 months.

elim: Results are stable over months, not a sudden decline.
eGFR is above 60.
Persistent haematuria and albuminuria are evidence of kidney damage.
Would not cause persistent haematuria and albuminuria for 6 months.

steps.x: B: Chronic kidney disease stage 2. CKD = kidney damage or reduced function for 3 months or more; eGFR 60 to 89 with damage = stage 2.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has a renal ultrasound because his mother has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. It shows multiple cysts in both kidneys. His BP is 132/82 mmHg. His eGFR is 98 mL/min/1.73m² on two occasions 4 months apart and his urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely CKD stage?
o: No CKD, as eGFR is normal
questions.e: Stage 1 CKD is an eGFR over 90 with supporting evidence of kidney damage, here hereditary polycystic disease on imaging. Without such evidence, a normal eGFR is not CKD.

steps.x: eGFR over 90 with hereditary structural kidney disease.

elim: Hereditary kidney disease with structural abnormality is evidence of damage.
Would need an eGFR of 60 to 89.
Would need an eGFR of 45 to 59.
Would need an eGFR under 15.

steps.x: B: Stage 1. Stage 1: eGFR over 90 with supporting evidence of kidney damage.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has 3 months of tiredness, constant itching, poor appetite with nausea and swollen ankles. She looks pale. Her BP is 168/94 mmHg. Her eGFR is 11 mL/min/1.73m², having been 13 and 16 mL/min/1.73m² over the last 6 months.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: eGFR under 15 is stage 5 (established renal failure); fatigue, pruritus, nausea, fluid retention, hypertension and pallor are late features of CKD.

steps.x: Late uraemic features with eGFR under 15 over months.

elim: The decline is gradual over 6 months.
Would need an eGFR of 30 to 44.
Would need an eGFR of 15 to 29.
Does not cause months of itching and oedema.

steps.x: D: Chronic kidney disease stage 5. Stage 5 = eGFR under 15 (established kidney failure); late features are fatigue, pruritus, nausea, oedema, pallor.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 37 mL/min/1.73m² at his annual review. It was 39 mL/min/1.73m² four months ago. His ACR is 6 mg/mmol. He feels well. His BP is 138/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An eGFR under 60 on two occasions at least 90 days apart confirms CKD; 30 to 44 is stage 3b.

steps.x: eGFR under 60 on two occasions more than 90 days apart.

elim: Stable results 4 months apart, not a sudden rise in creatinine.
Would need an eGFR of 60 to 89.
Would need an eGFR of 45 to 59.
Would need an eGFR of 15 to 29.

steps.x: D: Chronic kidney disease stage 3b. Stage 3b = eGFR 30 to 44.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with CKD stage 4 attends for routine bloods. She takes ramipril and amlodipine and follows no special diet. She feels well. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
questions.e: Advanced CKD reduces potassium excretion, and ACE inhibitors add to this, so hyperkalaemia is common. CKD causes hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia.

steps.x: Advanced CKD plus an ACE inhibitor.

elim: CKD tends to cause hypocalcaemia.
Can occur but is not the classic finding.
The kidneys retain potassium in CKD, especially on an ACE inhibitor.
CKD causes phosphate retention, not loss.

steps.x: B: Hyperkalaemia. Deranged kidney function in CKD: high potassium, high creatinine and urea.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man on haemodialysis for 6 years falls from standing and fractures his hip. He has aching bones. He does not take steroids. His adjusted calcium is 2.10 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 2.3 mmol/L (0.8–1.5) and PTH 68 pmol/L (1.6–6.9).
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his fracture?
questions.e: Low calcium and high phosphate in CKD drive secondary hyperparathyroidism, which causes renal bone disease and fragility fractures. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism gives a high calcium.

steps.x: Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH and a fragility fracture in ESRD.

elim: No cancer history, and the bloods fit renal bone disease.
Causes a very high ALP with normal calcium and phosphate.
Gives high calcium and low phosphate.
Would give a high calcium, not low.

steps.x: D: Secondary hyperparathyroidism. CKD-induced secondary hyperparathyroidism causes renal bone disease and fragility fractures.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman on haemodialysis has taken calcium acetate with meals for 3 years. She now has painful, firm skin nodules on her thighs. Her adjusted calcium is 2.78 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and phosphate 2.0 mmol/L (0.8–1.5). A plain X-ray of her pelvis shows extensive arterial calcification.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypercalcaemia and vascular calcification?
questions.e: Calcium-based phosphate binders such as calcium acetate can cause hypercalcaemia and, with a high phosphate, drive vascular calcification; sevelamer is a non-calcium alternative.

steps.x: Calcium-based binder with high calcium and phosphate and vascular calcification.

elim: Gives high calcium with low phosphate.
Causes hypercalcaemia but not on this background.
A non-calcium binder; it does not raise calcium.
Causes low, not high, calcium.

steps.x: A: Calcium-based phosphate binder. Calcium-based binders risk hypercalcaemia and vascular calcification; sevelamer avoids this.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with CKD stage 4 has 4 months of tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. She is pale. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and there is a soft ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Her ferritin, B12 and folate are normal. She has no blood loss.
questions.q: Which full blood count result is most likely?
questions.e: Anaemia of CKD is normocytic because reduced erythropoietin lowers red cell production without changing cell size; fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnoea, tachycardia and a flow murmur are typical.

clues: ferritin, B12 and folate are normal
steps.x: Advanced CKD, anaemia symptoms, flow murmur and normal haematinics.

elim: Microcytic, suggesting iron deficiency, but her ferritin is normal.
Macrocytic, suggesting B12 or folate deficiency, which are normal.
Normal, which does not fit her symptoms.
Polycythaemia, not anaemia.

steps.x: E: Hb 89 g/L, MCV 88 fL. Anaemia of CKD is normocytic, from reduced erythropoietin.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with CKD stage 4 has 6 months of aching pain in her hips and ribs and difficulty rising from a chair. She walks with a waddling gait. Her adjusted calcium is 2.08 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 1.9 mmol/L (0.8–1.5), ALP raised and PTH raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: CKD-mineral bone disease includes osteomalacia from reduced calcitriol, causing bone pain, proximal myopathy and a waddling gait with low calcium and raised ALP and PTH. Osteoporosis has normal bloods.

steps.x: Bone pain, proximal myopathy and waddling gait with low calcium, high phosphate, ALP and PTH.

elim: Would usually give a high calcium and normal ALP.
Does not cause proximal myopathy and these bloods.
Gives normal calcium, phosphate and ALP.
Causes stiffness with high ESR and normal bone chemistry.

steps.x: A: CKD-mineral bone disease with osteomalacia. CKD-MBD includes osteomalacia: bone pain, proximal myopathy, waddling gait.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD stage 4 has been taking metformin 1 g twice daily for years without review. He is admitted with vomiting, abdominal pain and rapid deep breathing. His capillary glucose is 8.4 mmol/L and ketones 0.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his acidosis?
questions.e: Metformin accumulates when kidney function is poor and causes lactic acidosis, so it is contraindicated in significant CKD; low ketones exclude DKA.

steps.x: Metformin in advanced CKD with metabolic acidosis and low ketones.

elim: Ketones are low.
Glucose is only mildly raised and HHS does not cause marked acidosis.
Deep, rapid breathing lowers CO2; this is a metabolic acidosis.
No history of overdose.

steps.x: C: Metformin accumulation causing lactic acidosis. Metformin is contraindicated in significant CKD: it accumulates and causes lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes has been on haemodialysis for 4 years. He smokes and has a raised cholesterol. The renal team discuss his long-term risks at his annual review. His BP is 152/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of death in patients like him?
questions.e: Cardiovascular disease is a key complication of CKD, and ischaemic heart disease is the most common cause of death in haemodialysis patients, which is why all CKD patients get a statin.

steps.x: Dialysis patient with diabetes, smoking and high cholesterol.

elim: Important but less common than cardiac death.
Can cause sudden death but is less common than IHD.
Smoking raises the risk, but IHD is far more common in dialysis patients.
Rare in patients receiving dialysis.

steps.x: C: Ischaemic heart disease. CKD greatly raises cardiovascular risk; IHD is the commonest cause of death on haemodialysis.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman had a deceased-donor kidney transplant 7 weeks ago. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisolone. She has missed several doses because of vomiting. Her creatinine has risen from 105 to 190 µmol/L over 4 days and the graft is tender. Her temperature is 37.6°C. Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and good blood flow.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the rise in creatinine?
questions.e: Acute graft rejection typically occurs in the first few months after transplant, especially with missed immunosuppression, giving a rising creatinine and a tender graft. Hyperacute rejection happens within hours.

clues: no hydronephrosis and good blood flow
steps.x: Missed immunosuppression in the first months, tender graft, rising creatinine.

elim: Develops over years, not weeks.
Occurs within minutes to hours of surgery.
Ultrasound shows good blood flow.
Ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.

steps.x: A: Acute graft rejection. Acute rejection typically occurs in the first few months after transplant.

questions.stem: A 26 year old competitive bodybuilder has an eGFR of 56 mL/min/1.73m² at a sports medicine check. He takes creatine supplements and ate a large steak the night before the test. He is well, his BP is 124/76 mmHg and his urine dipstick and ACR are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his low eGFR?
o: High creatinine from muscle mass and meat intake
questions.e: A large muscle mass or eating red meat the night before can raise creatinine and make eGFR inaccurately low; the test should be repeated without meat for 12 hours and CKD needs a persistent fall over 90 days.

steps.x: Large muscle mass, creatine and red meat before the test.

elim: He is well with normal urine and BP; the creatinine reflects muscle and diet.
Needs a persistently low eGFR over 90 days, and his urine is normal.
He has no diabetes.
Unlikely in a young normotensive man.

steps.x: D: High creatinine from muscle mass and meat intake. eGFR is calculated from creatinine; muscle mass and red meat raise creatinine and underestimate eGFR.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman weighing 46 kg has an eGFR of 48 mL/min/1.73m². She has new atrial fibrillation and the team want to calculate the correct dose of a direct oral anticoagulant. Her creatinine is 98 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate measure of her kidney function for drug dosing?
o: Creatinine clearance by the Cockcroft-Gault formula
questions.e: The Cockcroft-Gault formula uses age, sex, creatinine and weight to give creatinine clearance, which is used for dosing many drugs such as DOACs, especially in small, older patients.

steps.x: Low body weight, older age, drug dosing.

elim: Does not use weight and can overestimate function in a small, older patient.
Varies with hydration and protein intake.
Measures albuminuria, not filtration.
Detects blood and protein, not filtration.

steps.x: A: Creatinine clearance by the Cockcroft-Gault formula. Cockcroft-Gault uses age, sex, creatinine and weight to estimate creatinine clearance for drug dosing.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a creatinine of 140 µmol/L. The laboratory reports eGFR using the MDRD equation. The request form gives his creatinine, age and sex, but the laboratory needs one more piece of information.
questions.q: Which additional information does the MDRD equation need?
questions.e: The MDRD equation uses Creatinine, Age, Gender and Ethnicity (CAGE); weight is used in the Cockcroft-Gault formula.

steps.x: MDRD variables: CAGE.

elim: Not part of the equation.
Not part of the MDRD equation.
Needed for a 24-hour creatinine clearance, not MDRD.
Used in Cockcroft-Gault, not MDRD.

steps.x: B: Ethnicity. MDRD uses CAGE: Creatinine, Age, Gender, Ethnicity.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with hypertension has an early morning ACR of 35 mg/mmol. Her eGFR is 66 mL/min/1.73m². Her GP wants a quick bedside test to look for haematuria as further evidence of kidney damage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test?
questions.e: A urine dipstick is a quick confirmatory test for haematuria and proteinuria, which, if persistent, are evidence of kidney damage.

clues: quick bedside test to look for haematuria
steps.x: Raised ACR; confirm haematuria.

elim: Not relevant.
Not first-line to detect haematuria.
Not a bedside test.
Already measured and does not show haematuria.

steps.x: E: Urine dipstick. Urine dipstick is a confirmatory test for haematuria and proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a creatinine of 420 µmol/L found when he registers with a new GP. There are no earlier results. He has had itching and tiredness for months, and his Hb is 92 g/L. His BP is 166/96 mmHg. His bladder is not palpable.
questions.q: Which investigation would best distinguish chronic kidney disease from acute kidney injury?
questions.e: Renal ultrasound distinguishes CKD from AKI: bilaterally shrunken kidneys show long-standing irreversible damage. Potassium and dipstick findings occur in both.

steps.x: No baseline creatinine; symptoms suggest long-standing disease.

elim: Does not show the kidneys.
Invasive and not the first test for chronicity.
Can be high in both.
Abnormal in both.

steps.x: C: Renal ultrasound. Bilaterally shrunken kidneys on ultrasound are typical of CKD; normal-sized kidneys suggest AKI.

questions.stem: Two women with diabetic kidney disease both have an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73m². Woman A has an ACR of 2 mg/mmol and woman B has an ACR of 140 mg/mmol. Both have a BP of 136/84 mmHg and similar HbA1c.
questions.q: Which is the most likely difference in their outlook?
o: Both have the same risk because eGFR is equal
Woman A has a higher risk of progression
Woman B has a higher risk of progression
Woman B's ACR will fall without treatment
questions.e: Proteinuria is a marker of worse prognosis in CKD, so woman B, with heavy albuminuria, has a higher risk of progression and cardiovascular disease despite the same eGFR.

steps.x: Same eGFR, very different proteinuria.

elim: Proteinuria adds risk independent of eGFR.
Her ACR is normal.
Albuminuria tends to rise without treatment.
Both have an eGFR under 60.

steps.x: D: Woman B has a higher risk of progression. Proteinuria is a marker of worse prognosis in CKD.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has had hypertension for 6 years, treated with amlodipine. His eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73m². His GP wants to screen for kidney damage as part of his annual review. His BP is 144/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: An early morning urine ACR is the first-line test to detect albuminuria in people at risk of CKD such as those with hypertension; dipsticks miss microalbuminuria.

steps.x: Screening a hypertensive patient for kidney damage.

elim: Cumbersome and not first-line.
Less sensitive for microalbuminuria.
Invasive and not a screening test.
Does not detect kidney albumin loss.

steps.x: B: Early morning urine albumin:creatinine ratio. First-line: early morning urine ACR.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has CKD stage 3a from hypertensive nephrosclerosis. His ACR is 12 mg/mmol. He takes ramipril and amlodipine. His clinic BP is 148/92 mmHg on repeated readings. He does not have diabetes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate clinic BP target?
questions.e: In CKD the BP target is below 140/90 mmHg, lowered to below 130/80 mmHg when proteinuria is significant (ACR 70 mg/mmol or more).

steps.x: CKD without heavy proteinuria (ACR under 70).

elim: Too low; risks hypotension and falls.
The target for over-80s without CKD, too lenient here.
The threshold for stage 2 hypertension, not a target.
Lower than recommended in CKD without heavy proteinuria.

steps.x: C: Below 140/90 mmHg. BP target in CKD is 140/90, lower (130/80) if proteinuria is significant.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has two early morning ACRs of 4.6 and 5.0 mg/mmol, 2 months apart. Her eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73m² and her BP is 124/76 mmHg. She takes insulin only. She is not planning a pregnancy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: In diabetes, an ACR above 3 mg/mmol (above 3.5 mg/mmol in women, 2.5 mg/mmol in men) is an indication for an ACE inhibitor even with normal BP, to reduce albuminuria and slow progression.

steps.x: Diabetic woman with ACR above 3.5 mg/mmol and normal BP.

elim: Her ACR is already above the treatment threshold.
Does not reduce albuminuria.
Does not have the renoprotective effect of an ACE inhibitor.
Not first-line for albuminuria.

steps.x: E: Start an ACE inhibitor. In diabetes, start an ACE inhibitor if ACR is raised (over 3 mg/mmol; over 3.5 in women), even if BP is normal.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with type 2 diabetes has CKD stage 3a and an ACR of 62 mg/mmol. He has taken the maximum tolerated dose of ramipril for 6 months. His HbA1c is 52 mmol/mol on metformin. His BP is 132/80 mmHg and potassium is 4.9 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?
questions.e: For proteinuric CKD (ACR over 30 mg/mmol), an SGLT-2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin is added to an ACE inhibitor; it slows progression independent of glucose control. Dual ACE inhibitor and ARB therapy is not recommended.

steps.x: Proteinuric CKD on maximum ACE inhibitor.

elim: His BP is controlled; it does not reduce proteinuria.
Lowers glucose but has no renoprotective effect.
Raises potassium, which is already 4.9 mmol/L, and is not first choice.
Dual ACE inhibitor and ARB blockade is not recommended.

steps.x: B: Dapagliflozin. ACR over 30: ACE inhibitor plus SGLT-2 inhibitor; renoprotection is independent of glucose control.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has IgA nephropathy. He does not have diabetes. His eGFR is 68 mL/min/1.73m² and his ACR is 48 mg/mmol on two occasions. His BP is 128/78 mmHg. He takes no regular drugs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
questions.e: An ACR over 30 mg/mmol, with or without diabetes, is an indication for an ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril, even if BP is normal, because it reduces proteinuria and slows nephron loss.

steps.x: Proteinuric CKD with normal BP, no diabetes.

elim: Lowers BP but does not reduce proteinuria.
Not first-line for proteinuric CKD.
Not renoprotective.
ACE inhibitors are used even in normotensive proteinuric CKD.

steps.x: D: Lisinopril. ACR over 30 regardless of diabetes: start an ACE inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman with CKD stage 3b has painful osteoarthritis of the knees. She asks her GP for something stronger than paracetamol and mentions that her friend takes naproxen. She takes ramipril and furosemide.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Avoid naproxen and use topical NSAID or other non-oral options
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with omeprazole
questions.e: Slowing CKD progression includes avoiding nephrotoxic drugs such as oral NSAIDs, especially with an ACE inhibitor and diuretic; topical NSAIDs are a safer option for knee osteoarthritis.

steps.x: CKD on an ACE inhibitor and diuretic, considering an NSAID.

elim: Oral NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and should be avoided in CKD.
Also an oral NSAID; avoid in CKD.
Nephrotoxic and raises cardiovascular risk.
COX-2 inhibitors are also nephrotoxic.

steps.x: A: Avoid naproxen and use topical NSAID or other non-oral options. Slow progression: avoid nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man with end-stage kidney disease from IgA nephropathy has been on haemodialysis for 2 years. He has no other illnesses, works full time and his sister is a compatible donor. He finds dialysis restricts his life.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
o: Increase haemodialysis to 5 sessions a week
questions.e: Kidney transplant is the definitive treatment for end-stage renal disease; haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis are used before that.

steps.x: Young, fit ESRD patient with a donor.

elim: Inappropriate for a young, fit man.
Dialysis is not definitive.
Still dialysis, not definitive.
Used for ADPKD, not IgA nephropathy.

steps.x: C: Kidney transplant. Kidney transplant is definitive for ESRD; dialysis bridges until then.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman had a kidney transplant 2 years ago. She notices her gums have become swollen and overgrown and that she has more hair on her face and arms. Her creatinine has risen slightly. She takes immunosuppressants, amlodipine and atorvastatin.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Ciclosporin causes gingival hypertrophy, hypertrichosis and nephrotoxicity. Amlodipine can also cause gum overgrowth, but it does not explain the hair growth and rising creatinine.

clues: gums have become swollen and overgrown
more hair on her face and arms
steps.x: Gingival hypertrophy, hypertrichosis and nephrotoxicity.

elim: Causes myalgia, not gum overgrowth and hair growth.
Causes bone marrow suppression, not gum overgrowth.
Causes diarrhoea and marrow suppression, not hirsutism.
Causes Cushingoid features but not gum overgrowth with nephrotoxicity.

steps.x: C: Ciclosporin. Ciclosporin: gingival hypertrophy, hypertrichosis, nephrotoxicity.

questions.stem: A 45 year old fair-skinned man had a kidney transplant 5 years ago and takes tacrolimus and azathioprine. He works outdoors as a gardener. At transplant clinic he asks about his long-term health risks. His graft function is stable.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Daily sun protection and regular skin checks
Use sunbeds to maintain vitamin D
questions.e: Transplant recipients on immunosuppression have a 3 to 5 times higher risk of skin malignancy, so sun protection and regular skin surveillance are essential. Stopping immunosuppression causes rejection.

steps.x: Immunosuppressed transplant patient with high sun exposure.

elim: Not a specific transplant recommendation.
Would risk graft rejection.
Would cause rejection; it is lifelong.
Increases skin cancer risk.

steps.x: B: Daily sun protection and regular skin checks. Transplant recipients have a 3 to 5 times higher risk of skin cancer.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with CKD stage 4 has a Hb of 88 g/L with normal MCV. He was given intravenous iron 2 months ago. His ferritin is now 380 µg/L and transferrin saturation 28%. B12 and folate are normal. He is tired and breathless on exertion.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: In anaemia of CKD, iron is corrected first; once ferritin and transferrin saturation are adequate, an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent such as subcutaneous darbepoetin alfa replaces the missing erythropoietin.

steps.x: Anaemia of CKD with iron stores corrected.

elim: Not needed at Hb 88 g/L without severe symptoms.
Iron stores are already replete.
Iron is already replete.
Folate is normal.

steps.x: E: Subcutaneous darbepoetin alfa. Correct iron first, then subcutaneous erythropoietin (e.g. darbepoetin alfa).

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman on haemodialysis has a Hb of 64 g/L after a gastrointestinal bleed that has now stopped. She is breathless at rest and dizzy. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 102/60 mmHg. She already receives darbepoetin alfa.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Increase the darbepoetin dose and recheck in 4 weeks
questions.e: In severe anaemia (Hb under 70 g/L) in a patient on renal replacement therapy, red cell transfusion is given; erythropoietin and iron are too slow.

steps.x: Severe symptomatic anaemia on renal replacement therapy.

elim: Too slow for severe symptomatic anaemia.
Too slow for severe symptomatic anaemia.
Not indicated.
Not indicated.

steps.x: D: Red cell transfusion. Transfuse if Hb is under 70 g/L in severe anaemia on renal replacement therapy.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with CKD stage 3b has aching bones. Her adjusted calcium is 2.15 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 14 pmol/L (1.6–6.9) and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 18 nmol/L (50–125). Her phosphate is normal. She rarely goes outdoors.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.e: Vitamin D deficiency in CKD is corrected first with colecalciferol or ergocalciferol; activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol) is reserved for secondary hyperparathyroidism in ESRD.

steps.x: Vitamin D deficiency in CKD 3b with mildly raised PTH.

elim: Used for secondary hyperparathyroidism in ESRD; correct simple vitamin D deficiency first.
Used for refractory hyperparathyroidism, not first-line.
For tertiary or refractory hyperparathyroidism.
Her phosphate is normal.

steps.x: C: Colecalciferol. Correct vitamin D deficiency first with colecalciferol (D3) or ergocalciferol (D2).

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has been on haemodialysis for 3 years. His vitamin D stores have been replaced. His adjusted calcium is 2.12 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 1.6 mmol/L on a binder, and PTH is 54 pmol/L (1.6–6.9) and rising.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: In ESRD, the kidneys cannot 1-alpha-hydroxylate vitamin D, so secondary hyperparathyroidism is treated with alfacalcidol, an activated vitamin D that needs no renal activation.

clues: vitamin D stores have been replaced
steps.x: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in ESRD despite replete vitamin D.

elim: A calcium-based binder risking vascular calcification; does not supply active vitamin D.
Needs renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation, which his kidneys cannot do.
Also needs renal activation.
For tertiary or refractory disease, not first-line.

steps.x: A: Alfacalcidol. Alfacalcidol is already 1-alpha-hydroxylated, so works without kidney activation.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with CKD stage 4 has a phosphate of 1.9 mmol/L (0.8–1.5) on routine bloods. His adjusted calcium is 2.24 mmol/L and PTH is mildly raised. He eats a lot of processed food, dairy and cola. He is not on any phosphate-lowering treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line management?
questions.e: Hyperphosphataemia in CKD is managed first with dietary phosphate restriction (dietitian review); binders such as sevelamer come next if diet alone fails.

steps.x: Hyperphosphataemia with a high-phosphate diet, untreated.

elim: Raises phosphate absorption and is not first-line here.
A binder, used after diet; calcium-based binders risk calcification.
Not indicated.
A binder used if diet alone is not enough.

steps.x: C: Dietary phosphate restriction. Hyperphosphataemia: reduce dietary phosphate first-line, then binders such as sevelamer.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with CKD stage 4 has 2 weeks of increasing ankle swelling and breathlessness lying flat. She adds salt to all her food. She has pitting oedema to the knees and fine basal crackles. Her BP is 162/90 mmHg and potassium is 5.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Fluid overload in CKD is managed with loop diuretics such as furosemide plus a low-salt renal diet; spironolactone risks hyperkalaemia.

clues: adds salt to all her food
steps.x: Fluid overload in CKD with high salt intake.

elim: Would worsen fluid overload.
Her potassium is already high-normal.
Raises potassium in CKD and is not first choice here.
Not an emergency treatment for fluid overload.

steps.x: A: Furosemide and a low-salt diet. Manage fluid overload with diuretics and a low-salt renal diet.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Her eGFR has fallen from 82 to 62 mL/min/1.73m² over 2 years and her kidneys are enlarging rapidly on imaging. Her BP is controlled on ramipril. She is not pregnant.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to slow progression of her kidney disease?
questions.e: Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, reduces the rate of progression in rapidly progressing ADPKD by slowing cyst growth.

steps.x: Rapidly progressing ADPKD.

elim: Treats secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Reduces cardiovascular risk, not cyst growth.
Treats anaemia.
Treats hyperphosphataemia.

steps.x: E: Tolvaptan. Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 antagonist) slows progression in ADPKD.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man had his diabetes controlled tightly and his BP lowered to target 5 years ago, but his eGFR continues to fall slowly. He asks why his kidney function keeps getting worse.
questions.q: Which best explains the ongoing decline?
questions.e: CKD involves progressive, irreversible loss of functioning nephrons; remaining nephrons hyperfilter and are damaged in turn, so GFR keeps falling and excretory, endocrine and homeostatic functions are impaired.

steps.x: Ongoing decline despite controlling the cause.

elim: Nephrons cannot regenerate.
Nothing suggests infection.
CKD is irreversible.
CKD does not recover.

steps.x: B: Progressive loss of functioning nephrons. CKD is progressive, irreversible loss of functioning nephrons, lowering GFR.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with CKD stage 4 has a low adjusted calcium of 2.06 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). Her diet contains adequate calcium and her 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her low calcium?
o: Excess calcium excretion in the urine
High PTH causing bone uptake of calcium
questions.e: In CKD the kidneys make less active calcitriol, so intestinal calcium absorption falls and calcium drops even with normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D and adequate intake.

steps.x: Normal vitamin D stores but advanced CKD.

elim: CKD reduces, not increases, urinary calcium.
PTH releases calcium from bone.
Not the main cause in CKD.
Her diet is adequate.

steps.x: E: Reduced intestinal calcium absorption. Less calcitriol means less intestinal calcium absorption, so calcium falls.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with CKD stage 5 has a phosphate of 2.4 mmol/L (0.8–1.5) and a PTH of 48 pmol/L (1.6–6.9). A student asks how the high phosphate itself worsens his bone disease.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Phosphate suppresses calcitriol and stimulates PTH
questions.e: Reduced phosphate excretion in CKD causes hyperphosphataemia, which suppresses calcitriol and directly stimulates PTH, worsening bone disease and driving vascular calcification.

steps.x: Hyperphosphataemia with a raised PTH.

elim: It suppresses it.
High phosphate worsens bone disease.
It lowers calcitriol and so calcium absorption.
It stimulates PTH.

steps.x: E: Phosphate suppresses calcitriol and stimulates PTH. Reduced excretion raises phosphate, which suppresses calcitriol and stimulates PTH.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman without diabetes has proteinuric CKD and starts an SGLT-2 inhibitor. Her eGFR falls slightly in the first 2 weeks then stabilises. Her HbA1c is 38 mmol/mol and does not change.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the renoprotection?
o: Afferent arteriolar constriction by tubuloglomerular feedback
Direct dilation of the efferent arteriole
questions.e: SGLT-2 inhibitors increase sodium delivery to the macula densa, triggering tubuloglomerular feedback and afferent arteriolar constriction, which reduces glomerular hyperfiltration; this works independently of glucose control.

steps.x: Renoprotection in a non-diabetic, with a small early eGFR dip.

elim: This is how ACE inhibitors and ARBs work.
Her glucose is normal and unchanged.
Not the renoprotective mechanism.
This is how statins work.

steps.x: A: Afferent arteriolar constriction by tubuloglomerular feedback. More sodium reaches the macula densa, so the afferent arteriole constricts and hyperfiltration falls.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with CKD stage 4 has a normocytic anaemia with normal iron stores. A student asks which cells in the healthy kidney normally make the hormone he now lacks.
questions.q: Which cells normally produce this hormone?
questions.e: Erythropoietin is produced by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts; as the kidney fails, less is made, causing a normocytic anaemia. Juxtaglomerular cells make renin.

steps.x: Anaemia of CKD: erythropoietin deficiency.

elim: Form the filtration barrier.
Make renin.
Sense tubular sodium.
Make 1-alpha-hydroxylase for vitamin D activation.

steps.x: D: Peritubular interstitial fibroblasts. Erythropoietin is made by peritubular fibroblasts; their loss causes normocytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with diabetic kidney disease has a BP of 118/74 mmHg and an ACR of 40 mg/mmol. She is started on ramipril. Three months later her ACR is 18 mg/mmol and her BP is 114/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fall in her ACR?
questions.e: ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria and slowing nephron loss; this is why they are used even in normotensive proteinuric CKD.

steps.x: Proteinuria falls on an ACE inhibitor with almost no BP change.

elim: Would raise glomerular pressure.
Would raise ACR.
Not the mechanism.
Her BP barely changed; the benefit is intrarenal.

steps.x: E: Reduced intraglomerular pressure. Efferent dilation lowers intraglomerular pressure, so proteinuria and nephron loss fall.
